Day 2: seedling survival and CNDD

Author

Masatoshi Katabuchi

Published

October 22, 2026

Before you begin

Work individually, with nearby discussion if useful. Predict before running each comparison. All code is supplied; you do not need to write R or Stan code.

Use the prepared browser R environment. If access fails, open this HTML and the result sheet locally and answer the same questions. There is one core exercise today. Demonstrations and optional extensions are labelled. No installation or homework is required in the prepared browser environment. For optional local use, read Required packages and setup before class. No new model fitting is required for the core exercise.

By the end, you should be able to compare predicted survival probabilities and their uncertainty, and explain why a model should be checked against observations. The core exercise takes 15 minutes: predict 2, read/compare 6, write an interpretation 2, discuss 5. You may run the complete code or use the figures and result sheet; both routes answer the same questions. R and GLM experience are not prerequisites. The instructor explains the model and checks.

Core exercise: survival at low and high conspecific density

Purpose Compare survival probabilities and uncertainty, and explain the ecological result.
Computation Supplied posterior draws. Run the completed code or read the supplied figures; no new inference.
Data Seedlings and survivors in 60 simulated quadrats, with scaled conspecific density.

CNDD means conspecific negative density dependence. Today we ask whether seedling survival probability decreases with conspecific density. These simulated data illustrate the analysis. They are not observations from the research papers.

1. Predict the relationship

ndd <- make_ndd_data()
ggplot(ndd, aes(cons, suv/n, size=n)) + geom_point(alpha=.65) +
  labs(x="Conspecific density (scaled)", y="Observed proportion surviving",
       size="Seedlings")

Which density would you expect to have higher survival probability? Write a prediction. Each point is a quadrat. Different quadrats can contain different numbers of seedlings.

2. Read the model and curve

The model is the Day 1 binomial model with a density predictor:

s_i \sim \operatorname{Binomial}(n_i,p_i), \qquad \operatorname{logit}(p_i)=\alpha+\beta x_i.

The index i denotes a quadrat. x_i is scaled conspecific density. Both coefficients have independent Normal priors with mean 0 and SD 2.5. The model assumes a common probability within each quadrat and conditionally independent survival given that probability.

The instructor will explain this model. You do not need to memorise the logit formula or learn model-fitting syntax. Load the supplied result below, or use the curve already displayed in this reading copy.

fit <- course_fit("day2_ndd")
draws <- fit$draws
fit$source
#> [1] "precomputed"

precomputed means that these draws were generated before class. Loading them is not running a new fit. They match the data, model and priors described above.

Compare the two densities

plot_cndd(draws, ndd)

Compare low density (x=-1, one SD below the mean) with high density (x=1, one SD above the mean). Keep the fitted data, model, prior and draws fixed. Only the prediction density changes.

probabilities <- cndd_probabilities(draws)
probability_summary <- probabilities |> group_by(density) |>
  summarise(median=median(p), lower=quantile(p,.025), upper=quantile(p,.975))
probability_summary
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   density median lower upper
#>     <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1      -1  0.521 0.469 0.573
#> 2       1  0.170 0.130 0.217
plot_cndd_comparison(draws)

3. Explain the ecological result

Complete this sentence with values and intervals from the table:

Predicted survival probability is ___ (95% interval ___ to ) at low density, compared with (___ to ___) at high density, under this model.

Does knowing a survival probability also determine the exact number of survivors in the next group of seedlings? Explain in one sentence.

TipSolution and instructor notes

Predicted survival is 0.52 (0.47 to 0.57) at low density, and 0.17 (0.13 to 0.22) at high density. These intervals describe uncertainty about each probability. Future survivor counts also vary randomly given the probability and the number of seedlings.

The negative density coefficient is on the logit scale. It is neither a probability difference nor a percent reduction. Transform every draw before summarising the probability. Hold the predictor values fixed when comparing answers.

This fitted association alone does not establish causation or show why rare species are rare. Species differences enter the conceptual research example on Day 3.

Instructor demonstrations: prediction and model checking

The core exercise is complete. Read the following figures with the instructor; you do not need to run more code.

Predict new seedling groups

Keep the same fit and compare new groups of 20 seedlings at the two densities. The code draws a probability from the posterior and then generates a binomial count.

predictions <- cndd_predictions(draws, n=20, seed=20261022)
plot_cndd_predictions(predictions)

The probability interval and the distribution of future survivor counts answer different questions. Counts can vary even if we know the probability precisely.

Check the model against observations

Keep each observed quadrat’s density and seedling count fixed. Generate new survivor counts using posterior draws. Compare the density pattern and the range of replicated survival proportions with the observations.

replicates <- cndd_replicates(draws, ndd, seed=20261023)
plot_cndd_check(replicates, ndd)

Write one compatible feature and one pattern that would concern you. What would a systematic mismatch suggest? This is simulation from the existing posterior, not another model fit. Because these data were generated from this model, we do not require a visible failure. A compatible plot alone does not establish ecological adequacy. Light, soils, shared enemies and species differences may matter in a real study.

TipSolution and instructor notes

The orange intervals in the first check are intervals for replicated proportions, including binomial variation at each observed n_i. They differ from the interval for p_i in the fitted-curve plot. Some observed points can lie outside 95% intervals. Do not count all such points as model failures. Look for systematic patterns.

A discrepancy could involve the density relationship, missing conditions or dependence among seedlings. It is not a uniquely identified diagnosis of a single ecological mechanism. The SD summary is optional reference material below.

Optional reference and lecture illustration

The core exercise is complete. These sections support the lecture; skip them if time is short.

Prior scale: the Normal regression illustration

The lecture uses the Normal-response example from main.qmd to ask whether a slope of 100 is sensible for the displayed units and ranges. It is a short illustration, not a second analysis exercise.

plot_normal_prior_scale()

For y_i\sim\mathcal{N}(a x_i+b,\sigma), a slope prior a\sim\mathcal{N}(0,2.5) uses SD 2.5 in the units of y per unit x. In CNDD the coefficients are on the logit scale. The same numerical SD does not imply the same ecological change. In both models, judge the implied predictions in the units of the question.

Computation checks: instructor reference

course_diagnostics(fit)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 6
#>   max_rhat min_bulk_ess min_tail_ess divergent max_treedepth min_ebfmi
#>      <dbl>        <dbl>        <dbl>     <dbl>         <int>     <dbl>
#> 1     1.00        1698.        2123.         0             0      1.03
bayesplot::mcmc_trace(draws, pars=c("alpha","beta"))

The instructor checks traces, R-hat, bulk/tail ESS, divergences, treedepth and E-BFMI together. Students only need to distinguish two questions: did computation work, and does the model describe the observations? Memorising thresholds or repairing a sampler is not required. Healthy diagnostics do not establish ecological adequacy. The handwritten Stan model below is reference material, not a coding task.

NoteCompleted Stan model 
data {
  int<lower=0> N;               // number of quadrats
  array[N] int<lower=0> n;      // seedlings per quadrat
  array[N] int<lower=0> suv;    // survivors per quadrat
  vector[N] cons;               // conspecific density (scaled)
}

parameters {
  real alpha;                   // intercept (logit scale)
  real beta;                    // slope (logit scale)
}

model {
  // likelihood: logit(p) = alpha + beta * cons
  suv ~ binomial_logit(n, alpha + beta * cons);
  // priors
  alpha ~ normal(0, 2.5);
  beta ~ normal(0, 2.5);
}

Optional demonstration: fit the same model with brms

Purpose: connect the ecological model to one complete fitting command. Who/time: instructor demonstration, up to 3 minutes only if the core discussion is complete. Use a result prepared before class; omit rather than wait for compilation. Students with a validated environment may try this later by choice. It is not homework or a prerequisite for any task. No student installation is required.

brms translates an R formula into Stan; cmdstanr runs CmdStan. 0 + Intercept + cons gives an intercept at cons = 0 and a slope, both with independent Normal(0, 2.5) priors. This matches stan/logit_reg.stan; the usual centred-intercept specification need not impose the same intercept prior. The saved core fit is handwritten Stan, not a brms object.

Starter and instructions: run setup and core-data above, then this complete chunk only in a prepared environment. Keep the data, formula and priors fixed. Compilation and sampling are new computation; elapsed time is machine-dependent and has not been measured for the classroom server. This chunk is not executed when rendering the handout. Do not use Run All to start an optional fit.

library(brms)
elapsed <- system.time({
  fit_brms <- brm(
    suv | trials(n) ~ 0 + Intercept + cons,
    data=ndd, family=binomial(link="logit"),
    prior=set_prior("normal(0, 2.5)", class="b"),
    backend="cmdstanr", seed=20261022,
    chains=4, cores=1, iter=2000, warmup=1000, refresh=500
  )
})
elapsed
# Preserve chain/iteration identifiers when adapting names for course plots.
brms_draws <- posterior::subset_draws(
  posterior::as_draws_df(fit_brms), variable=c("b_Intercept", "b_cons"))
names(brms_draws)[names(brms_draws) == "b_Intercept"] <- "alpha"
names(brms_draws)[names(brms_draws) == "b_cons"] <- "beta"
brms_result <- list(draws=brms_draws, data=ndd_stan_data(ndd), source="live-brms",
            diagnostics=fit_brms$fit$diagnostic_summary())
course_diagnostics(brms_result)
bayesplot::mcmc_trace(brms_draws, pars=c("alpha", "beta"))
plot_cndd_comparison(brms_draws)

Compare: expect the same broad density relationship and similar probability intervals as the supplied fit, with Monte Carlo variation. Report the source as live-brms; loading the saved result is precomputed. Check actual live diagnostics before interpreting a new fit. An error or a problematic fit does not invalidate your completed core exercise; stop and return to the supplied figures.

TipSolution and instructor notes

The likelihood, seed data and independent coefficient priors match the core model; individual draws need not match. b_Intercept maps to alpha, b_cons to beta. Keep chain identifiers for diagnostics. Inspect parameter-level R-hat and ESS, traces and chain-level sampler diagnostics. Never report healthy stored diagnostics as diagnostics for a problematic live run. Validate compilation, sampling and plotting in a fresh instructor account before showing this optional demonstration.

Optional reference: variation across quadrats

plot_cndd_spread_check(replicates, ndd)

This compares one SD of observed survival proportions with SDs of replicated data. It is not a posterior distribution for the observed SD. Skip if time is short.

Optional extension: a probability difference

Use the same fit and paired posterior draws. Compute high-density minus low-density survival probability, then interpret the distribution. No refit is needed.

p_low <- plogis(draws$alpha-draws$beta)
p_high <- plogis(draws$alpha+draws$beta)
course_interval(p_high-p_low)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>     mean median  lower  upper
#>    <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 -0.351 -0.351 -0.424 -0.273
mean(p_high-p_low < 0)
#> [1] 1
TipSolution and instructor notes

A negative difference means lower predicted survival at high density for the specified comparison. The interval comes from paired differences, not from subtracting interval endpoints. Its units are probability points, not an odds ratio.

Reflection

What would you check before using this analysis on your own data? Tomorrow we ask how mother trees and species can differ while sharing information.
